segments.title: How four G3 hulls might become aircraft carriers
segments.summary: A speculative G3 conversion shows how altered treaty tonnage could reshape British carrier strength and provoke matching American and Japanese responses.
segments.body: A fan-drawn G3 carrier opens a counterfactual in which all four hulls become aircraft carriers for the Royal Navy. The scenario uses the proposed 10:10:7 ratio and a 33,000-ton carrier ceiling, rather than the historical treaty settlement. The drawing separates the command island forward from the funnel island aft, though a real British conversion might instead have used a single island farther aft. Four British conversions would probably have affected American and Japanese plans, turning each navy's carrier policy into part of a wider competition.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses four G3 carrier conversions, the proposed tonnage ratio, and the twin-island drawing.

segments.title: Why France and Italy received different capital-ship and carrier ratios
segments.summary: France and Italy received smaller capital-ship shares but larger carrier shares, showing that the familiar 5:5:3 formula did not govern every treaty category identically.
segments.body: The familiar 5:5:3 formula applied to Britain, the United States, and Japan, but it did not describe every category or signatory. France and Italy began near 1.75 in the original comparison, settled around 1.66 for capital ships, and received roughly 2.2 for carriers. The figures differ because capital ships and aircraft carriers were the only categories governed by these ratios. Cruisers and smaller vessels were outside the same allocation, so the headline ratio alone cannot reconstruct treaty strength.

evidence.note: The transcript compares the original 5:5:3 and 1.75 ratios with the different French and Italian capital-ship and carrier allocations.

segments.title: Why the 35,000-ton battleship limit looked unrealistic
segments.summary: The historical 35,000-ton ceiling is criticized for forcing every navy below the displacement its own requirements appeared to demand.
segments.body: Contemporary design work was already clustering around roughly 40,000 to 43,000 tons, which made a 35,000-ton ceiling inadequate for the requirements of every major navy. Knowingly forcing poorer designs would shift the cost of idealistic arms limitation onto sailors in a future war. Equal constraints did not make the danger morally equal because each government remained responsible for its own personnel. The proposed alternative therefore starts from a practical premise: if complete disarmament is unattainable, a peace-minded treaty must still permit viable warships.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the 35,000-ton limit with larger design requirements and argues for realistic preparation.

segments.title: Why the counterfactual keeps a 16-inch gun ceiling
segments.summary: The alternative treaty retains the historical 16-inch maximum because larger-gun Queen Elizabeth ideas remained speculative rather than demonstrated design requirements.
segments.body: The counterfactual accepts the treaty's 16-inch gun maximum while rejecting its 35,000-ton displacement cap. An 18-inch-armed Queen Elizabeth-class design is presented as a speculative preference, alongside competing ideas for triple 15-inch mountings. Neither proposal was built, and the turret arrangements remain uncertain, so they do not supply firm evidence for a higher ceiling. The alternative retains a historical limit because the design case for change is weaker.

evidence.note: The transcript accepts the 16-inch limit while distinguishing speculative 18-inch Queen Elizabeth and triple 15-inch ideas from ships actually built.

segments.title: Japan's security case for a 7:10 fleet ratio
segments.summary: Japan sought enough strength to make an American attack uncertain, while recognizing that superior American industry would prevail in a long war.
segments.body: The historical 5:5:3 framework gave Japan three-fifths of American strength, while Japanese leaders wanted seven-tenths. They feared isolation after the end of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance and sought a fleet strong enough to make an opening attack prohibitively risky. The ratio could not overcome British or American industrial depth in a long war, but it could deny either power confidence in a quick first-round victory. Japan's relatively successful First World War experience also differed sharply from Europe's trauma, helping explain why the same treaty bargain looked different in Tokyo.

evidence.note: The transcript states the historical ratios, explains Japanese fear of attack, notes the alliance's end, and contrasts Japan's wartime experience with Europe's.

segments.title: Why an arms-control treaty cannot maximize one side's victory
segments.summary: A durable naval treaty must leave every signatory with enough advantage to prefer compliance over withdrawal or rearmament.
segments.body: American intelligence helped negotiators identify how far other powers could be pushed, but winning the bargain too decisively could destroy its durability. States comply while an arrangement remains in their interest. A signatory repeatedly held to its bare minimum eventually has little reason to preserve the agreement. A negotiator may therefore need to give up part of a possible national advantage to reduce the chance that a dissatisfied power later abandons the system.

evidence.note: The transcript links treaty durability to every nation's incentive to remain within it.

segments.title: A 42,000-ton capital-ship settlement with staged replacement
segments.summary: The proposed settlement raises the battleship ceiling to 42,000 tons, adopts a 20:20:14:8:8 distribution, and phases replacement by ship age.
segments.body: HMS Hood's reported displacement supplies the precedent for rounding the capital-ship ceiling to 42,000 tons while retaining 16-inch guns. Scaling Japan upward produces a proposed distribution of twenty ships each for Britain and the United States, fourteen for Japan, and eight each for France and Italy. The replacement rules extend a phased scheme offered to France and Italy to every signatory and prevent any navy from building more than one-fifth of its allowance at once. Ships laid down before 1914 with guns of 14 inches or less could be replaced from 1926, while pre-1914 ships with larger guns would wait until 1930. Ships laid down from 1914 through 1918 could follow from 1934. An eighteen-year service life for treaty ships would eventually sustain a regular construction rhythm.

evidence.note: The transcript states the 42,000-ton ceiling, revised ratios, and phased replacement dates.

segments.title: Why undersized capital ships would become death traps
segments.summary: A 42,000-ton, 16-inch-gun standard would make surviving 20,000-ton ships and pre-dreadnoughts dangerously ineffective.
segments.body: The revised ceiling changes the value of older and smaller capital ships, as well as the specifications of future construction. Roughly 20,000-ton vessels armed with 12- or 13-inch guns could not fight effectively against 42,000-ton ships carrying 16-inch guns. They would be little better than death traps, which would influence British, Japanese, and American choices about which ships to retain or replace first. The same logic leaves pre-dreadnoughts still further behind. To emphasize their obsolescence, the video argues that HMS Hood could defeat the world's combined surviving pre-dreadnought force.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts 20,000-ton ships with 12- or 13-inch guns against the proposed 42,000-ton, 16-inch standard, then uses HMS Hood to illustrate pre-dreadnought obsolescence.

segments.title: Why a steady shipbuilding drumbeat preserves naval capacity
segments.summary: Regular replacement spreads the cost of skilled labor, infrastructure, research, and surge capacity across more hulls than stop-start procurement.
segments.body: The treaty design is tied directly to industrial policy: Britain and the United States need recurring construction to retain the ability to build major warships. The Type 26 programs in Britain, Canada, and Australia provide a modern analogy for deliberately slow production that keeps yards and skills alive. Stop-start procurement forces a navy to pay repeatedly to rebuild industrial capability whenever it needs a new class. Individual ships can look expensive because each project carries part of the cost of complex infrastructure, research, accumulated experience, and future surge capacity. A larger continuous program spreads those costs across more hulls.

evidence.note: The transcript connects replacement timing, Type 26 production, industrial continuity, and per-hull costs.

segments.title: Why the treaty could permit forty-eight County-class cruisers
segments.summary: Washington capped cruiser size and gun caliber but not cruiser numbers, leaving British output constrained more by funding and industry than by the treaty itself.
segments.body: The Washington settlement capped cruiser displacement at 10,000 tons and guns at eight inches, but it set no total number. Britain could therefore have sustained six County-class heavy cruisers per year until the London Naval Treaty, potentially reaching forty-eight new ships plus the Hawkins class. A parallel light-cruiser program would make the counterfactual even larger. Government funding and shipyard capacity, rather than treaty law, would set the practical limits. The calculation separates formal arms-control rules from the budgets that determine whether a navy can exploit them.

evidence.note: The transcript notes the absence of a cruiser-number limit and calculates six County-class ships per year, forty-eight ships, the Hawkins class, and possible matching light-cruiser construction.

segments.title: G3 conversions and an alternative Royal Navy fast fleet
segments.summary: Alternative G3 completion and conversion choices produce an interwar fast fleet that includes Hood, Tiger, Renown, and Repulse.
segments.body: One illustrated scenario completes a G3 as a surface warship while converting three sister hulls into carriers. The imagined fast fleet also includes Hood, Tiger, Renown, and Repulse. Its ceremonial lineup places a G3 opposite Renown, Hood opposite Repulse, and the Jutland veteran Tiger between them. This formation turns abstract tonnage rules into a concrete picture of the fleet that different disposal and conversion choices could permit.

evidence.note: The transcript describes three G3 carriers, one completed G3, and the accompanying fast fleet.

segments.title: Carrier tonnage, conversions, and the transition to new builds
segments.summary: The alternative assigns carrier tonnage on a 10:10:7:4:4 ratio, keeps the eight-inch-gun ceiling, and phases converted hulls into purpose-built carriers.
segments.body: Treaty delegates appear unusually restrictive toward carriers even though no existing project approached the permitted maximum. The eight-inch gun ceiling is understandable because Furious, Courageous, and Glorious provided precedents for carrier hulls associated with 15- and 18-inch weapons, while negotiators still regarded gunfire as more practical than aircraft. The alternative allocation applies the 10:10:7:4:4 ratio to carrier tonnage and limits construction in progress to one-fifth of a navy's allowance. It sets a 33,000-ton unit ceiling, requires early carriers to be conversions, permits a mixed program after 1926, and allows wholly new construction after 1930. Replacement rules let pre-treaty conversions retire from 1930 and post-treaty conversions or pre-treaty new builds from 1934, while post-treaty new builds serve at least eighteen years. Because conversions use tonnage less efficiently per hull, the timetable forces a choice between obtaining airpower sooner and waiting for better purpose-built ships.

evidence.note: The transcript critiques historical carrier limits, explains the gun ceiling, sets out the alternative allocation and construction phases, and contrasts conversion efficiency with new builds.

segments.title: How one capital-ship category encouraged fast battleships
segments.summary: A single capital-ship category penalized fleets that operated both battleships and battlecruisers and encouraged the fast battleship, a type already foreshadowed by the Queen Elizabeth class.
segments.body: The treaty counted battleships and battlecruisers together as one capital-ship category. This disadvantaged Britain and Japan, which already operated both types, while the United States had no battlecruisers in service. Once a navy must choose one limited set of capital ships, speed and battle-line strength become more attractive in the same hull, making the fast battleship a predictable result. The Queen Elizabeth class already pointed in that direction and might have reached roughly 27 to 28 knots with small-tube boilers.

evidence.note: The transcript says the combined battleship and battlecruiser category disadvantaged Britain and Japan, encouraged the fast battleship, and identifies the Queen Elizabeth class as an early path toward it.

segments.title: A carrier-conversion loophole and the treaty's enforcement gap
segments.summary: The treaty's use of permissive conversion language suggests a possible new-build loophole whose practical restraint depended on political pressure rather than automatic enforcement.
segments.body: The wording says contracting powers may use two otherwise-scrapped ships for 33,000-ton carrier conversions. Because the clause says may rather than must, it can be read as permitting two large carriers built from scratch. Other signatories would probably have challenged an attempt to exploit that interpretation. The ambiguity exposes a wider weakness: in 1922 the treaty ultimately relied on the threat of war, even though few governments were likely to fight over a carrier clause.

evidence.note: The transcript examines the word may in the carrier clause, a possible new-build reading, and the weakness of enforcement by threat of war.

segments.title: Six British conversions and a six-Lexington carrier force
segments.summary: Higher treaty allowances open paths to six British battlecruiser conversions or all six Lexington-class hulls entering service as American carriers.
segments.body: The British calculation combines three Admiral-class conversions with Furious, Courageous, and Glorious, using 171,000 tons of a 330,000-ton allowance and leaving room for Argus, Eagle, Hermes, or other carriers. The American counterpart converts all six Lexington-class battlecruisers into Lexington, Constellation, Saratoga, Ranger, Constitution, and United States. Those six conversions would provide a powerful foundation while leaving room to build toward a ten-carrier allowance. The alternatives show how generous conversion rules could accelerate naval aviation well before the historical carrier race.

evidence.note: The transcript calculates British conversion tonnage and names a six-ship Lexington conversion fleet.

segments.title: Regional carrier ratios depend on fleet concentration
segments.summary: Japan could concentrate seven carriers in the western Pacific, but combined or reinforced Anglo-American forces could erase that local numerical advantage.
segments.body: The 10:10:7 allocation gives Japan a plausible local carrier advantage without global superiority. Seven Japanese carriers might concentrate in the western Pacific against perhaps five American carriers in the eastern Pacific and three British carriers in the Indian Ocean. Combining the British and American detachments produces an eight-to-seven balance before further reinforcement. Theater distribution and coalition concentration therefore matter as much as the treaty's headline fleet ratio.

evidence.note: The transcript compares Japanese, American, and British carrier concentrations across the Pacific and Indian Ocean.

segments.title: Shipbuilding as economic support and strategic resilience
segments.summary: Continued warship construction could advance technology, sustain employment, and leave the treaty powers better prepared for 1930s rearmament.
segments.body: A less restrictive treaty would keep money, technical experience, and productive infrastructure moving through national economies. That continuity could soften economic shocks and widen the industrial gap that later fascist rearmament would have to overcome. Continued building would also give treaty powers more confidence that they could meet their own requirements, while common limits prevent any one fleet from becoming overwhelmingly strong. Because cruisers are limited by size and gun caliber rather than total numbers, sustained cruiser orders could partly compensate for reduced battleship and carrier work when governments provide the funding.

evidence.note: The transcript links construction with technology, employment, infrastructure, deterrence, and cruiser output.

segments.title: Pacific fortification limits and Japanese insecurity
segments.summary: Restrictions on Japan's former German islands compounded its inferior fleet ratio by making recently won territories feel exposed to reversal.
segments.body: Britain and the United States retained stronger regional bases, while Japan could not fortify islands gained from Germany during the First World War. Many island positions could be bypassed operationally, but their vulnerability still mattered politically and emotionally. The settlement made Japan's wartime gains feel revocable because another power could seize them without facing a serious local cost. The revised clause permits modernization within each base's existing area, requires full disclosure, and allows defensive weapons up to eight-inch cruiser caliber. An attacker would face a meaningful obstacle, without giving Japan unlimited room to expand its bases.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Japan's fortification problem and reads the proposed modernization and defense clause.

segments.title: Why national emotion matters in treaty design
segments.summary: Treaty outcomes depend on collective fear, confidence, and humiliation as well as apparently rational calculations of tonnage and force ratios.
segments.body: States are communities whose policies are shaped by culture, worldview, and emotion. A classroom analogy explains how a group's shared mood can influence behavior even when its members remain individuals. The emotional legacy of Versailles then serves as a warning that a formally logical settlement can produce destabilizing resentment. Weimar Germany still had other possible futures, but accumulated grievance helped make it fertile ground for Nazism. With the United States outside the League of Nations, Britain, France, Italy, and Japan needed enough confidence and strength to support the interwar security order rather than feel bound or diminished by it.

evidence.note: The transcript connects collective emotion, Versailles, the League of Nations, and perceptions of naval strength.

segments.title: Balanced deterrence as the equitable treaty's goal
segments.summary: The final design gives each power enough viable ships and construction freedom to feel secure, but not enough superiority to attack confidently.
segments.body: The proposed system aims for a narrow political balance: each signatory should believe it gained enough to remain invested in the treaty, without gaining enough to exploit the others. Larger viable capital ships and revised ratios supply confidence, while continued construction supports employment, yards, and naval readiness. British or American building could proceed slowly enough to remain affordable, and American congressional reluctance would probably prevent a sustained Anglo-American naval race. Testing the balance across the Mediterranean, Atlantic, Indian Ocean, and Pacific suggests that every power could defend important interests, though none could concentrate without exposing another theater.

evidence.note: The transcript summarizes the balance principle and tests force distributions across several theaters.

segments.title: How a three-theatre Royal Navy constrains rival concentration
segments.summary: Distributing twenty-one British ships among home, Mediterranean, and Indian Ocean forces creates local vulnerabilities, but rival concentration exposes another theatre to coalition response.
segments.body: The headline ratio becomes a deployment problem if Britain uses 40,000-ton capital ships and fits twenty-one within its allowance. That permits three groups of seven for home waters, the Mediterranean, and the Indian Ocean. In the Mediterranean, eight Italian ships would outnumber the local British group by one, yet even four French ships would reverse the local balance. Japan could concentrate fourteen ships against seven British vessels in the Indian Ocean, but doing so would expose its other flank to a possible American force of ten in the Pacific. Interlocking regional commitments can therefore deter aggression even when no single navy is superior everywhere.

evidence.note: The transcript divides twenty-one British ships among three theatres and compares Mediterranean and Indo-Pacific concentration choices.

segments.title: How to build a historically bounded treaty counterfactual
segments.summary: The alternative treaty must grow from positions and precedents visible at the Washington conference rather than from an unconstrained ideal settlement.
segments.body: The counterfactual follows rules meant to keep it historically bounded. Any alternative must fit the conference's political context, the proposals actually discussed, and the decisions negotiators could plausibly have made. Judging the delegates against a settlement invented without those constraints would be historically unfair. The result is a moderate revision built from the participants' own logic, rather than a present-day wish list imposed on the past.

evidence.note: The transcript states that alternatives must remain grounded in the conference's actual context and ideas.
